note: The four 7th chords and the two triads on one root (sevenths-up:7): pressed in the chord boxes in pairs, named in the ear game by its button labels, then called out over a backing track that holds all four 7th chords. The root stays on G, since the chord kinds are the lesson; the ear game has no half-diminished answer, so that chord is heard in the chord boxes and the backing track only.

exercise.title: Four 7th chords and two triads
exercise.why: Each of the four 7th chords is a triad with a 7th on top, so hearing the three notes underneath first and the top note second tells them from the triads and from each other.

cells.text:
Press a chord box below to hear the chord. Press G and Gm, the two triads, then Gmaj7 and G7: the major triad with a 7th on top, a half step or a whole step under the octave.
Then press Gm7 and Gm7♭5: the minor triad with the lower 7th, and the same chord with its 5th lowered a half step.
Practice until you can name each of the six with your eyes closed.

Press Start in the game below to hear a chord on a new root each time. Pick Major, Minor, Dominant 7, Major 7 or Minor 7: Dominant 7 is the chord written 7, as in G7.
Listen to the three notes underneath first, major or minor, then for a 7th on top.
If two answers sound alike, press Replay in the game and listen only for the top note.

Press Play below to start the backing track: the four 7th chords on G, one bar each, in two orders. Look away from the chord boxes and call out the chord at each change, then look back to check.
Listen for the bar where the 5th drops: that is Gm7♭5, the half-diminished chord.
